summary:
Guinea's 2016 Penal Code, Article 274, punishes consensual same-sex conduct with six months to three years' imprisonment, a fine of GNF 500,000 to 1,000,000, or both. The provision replaced Article 325 of the 1998 Penal Code, which criminalised the same conduct through indecency provisions and set a lower minimum fine. Where the conduct involves violence or attempted violence, the sentence rises to five to ten years, and acts with a person under 21 carry the maximum penalty.

Enforcement reaches people who are not charged with conduct. Police arrest on the basis of clothing and appearance, and Article 274 functions as a standing basis for extortion, with release commonly secured by payment to officers. A 2024 Universal Periodic Review stakeholder submission reports LGBTQ people held for up to five days despite the 48-hour legal limit, most released only after paying bribes or fines. In 2023 the Office for the Protection of Women, Children, and Morals added a unit to investigate same-sex conduct. Security forces have arrested, harassed and used violence against LGBTQ people accused of disrupting social order. In 2016 and 2017 the organisation Afrique Arc-en-Ciel Conakry reported gay men jailed and fined for release.

Custody carries specific risk. LGBTQ people in detention are frequently abused, and transgender women are arrested and imprisoned on the stated pretext of protecting them from community violence, then held in male prisons where they often experience sexual violence.

Guinea has no legal gender recognition, so a trans visitor cannot obtain identity documents matching their gender, and no recognition of same-sex unions. A trans visitor in a relationship the law would read as same-sex has no route to partnership recognition.

The UPR submission describes a hostile, sometimes lethal environment with threats of physical violence and discrimination on grounds of orientation, gender identity and expression, and notes that widespread stigmatisation hinders reporting of violence. A survey covering 2021 to 2023 found 87 percent of Guineans would dislike or strongly dislike having a gay neighbour. The State Department's 2011 report described homosexuality as socially, religiously and culturally taboo with no LGBTQ organisations in the country; its 2023 report found that LGBTQ people are cast as part of a Western imperialist agenda attributed to the United States and France.
tangentialFactors:
Guinea's health law names sexual minorities without extending anti-discrimination protection. Law L/2024/001/CNT/SGG of 12 January 2024 on HIV Prevention, Care, and Protection defines members of sexual minorities to include gays, lesbians, bisexuals, intersex and transgender people whether or not they self-identify, and Ordinance No. 056/2009/PRG/SGG on HIV/AIDS lists sexual minorities as a vulnerable and marginalised group; no law protects LGBTQ people from discrimination in health services.

Section 9.9.30(b) of the Guinea Aeronautical Regulations (2022), issued by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, bars competent government agencies from using Passenger Name Record data that reveals an individual's sex life or sexual orientation, alongside racial, ethnic, political, religious, trade-union or health data. The text gives no further detail on entry screening, visa rules or border checks for trans or LGBTQ travellers.

In 2010 Prime Minister Lansana Kouyate stated that consensual same-sex activity was wrong and should be illegal and that sexual orientation should not be a human right. The State Department's 2011 report, in the same document that records criminalisation and societal discrimination, documents security-force torture and prison abuse.
localsOnly:
Adoption in Guinea is open to a couple married at least five years or to an unmarried person aged at least 30 where there is a 15-year age gap; the law does not specifically bar LGBTQ people from adopting.

LGBTQ Guineans face discrimination in healthcare, housing, education and employment. Families arrange forced heterosexual marriages, and religious, cultural and familial pressure is used to attempt to convert LGBTQ people, a pressure that falls heavily on younger people. Some LGBTQ Guineans have been internally displaced to escape areas whose religious and cultural norms endanger them.

LGBTQ organisations exist but cannot obtain legal recognition even though no law bars it, and most LGBTQ Guineans do not disclose publicly; there is no substantial political presence of openly LGBTQ people.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents how Article 274 is applied to foreign visitors specifically, or whether police stop, search or charge travellers on the basis of appearance at ports of entry.

The Guinea Aeronautical Regulations address PNR data handling only; the inventory contains no account of trans-specific screening, pat-down or secondary inspection practice at Conakry's airport or land borders.

The inventory contains no per-capita or comparative data on violence against transgender people in Guinea.

Whether the 2023 unit added to investigate same-sex conduct has produced prosecutions is not stated in the sources.
